title: Region Proposal by Guided Anchoring
venue: IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings - IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings

problem.summary: Modern detectors prepare anchors with a uniform sliding-window scheme over feature maps using a hand-picked set of scales and aspect ratios; this is inefficient because anchors are scattered over regions where objects are unlikely to exist, and it forces per-task manual anchor design while most anchors are irrelevant candidates.
statements: A fixed set of anchor scales and aspect ratios must be predefined for each problem, and a wrong design may hamper the speed and accuracy of the detector.
Maintaining high proposal recall requires a large number of anchors, most of which are false candidates irrelevant to the objects of interest.
A large number of anchors causes significant computational cost, especially when the proposal stage involves a heavy classifier.
Many anchors are placed in regions where the objects of interest are unlikely to exist.

evidence.quote: A neat set of anchors of fixed aspect ratios has to be predefined for different problems. A wrong design may hamper the speed and accuracy of the detector.
To maintain a sufficiently high recall for proposals, a large number of anchors are needed, while most of them correspond to false candidates that are irrelevant to the object of interests.
Meanwhile, a large number of anchors can lead to significant computational cost especially when the pipeline involves a heavy classifier in the proposal stage.
This scheme is inefficient, as many of the anchors are placed in regions where the objects of interest are unlikely to exist.

background.summary: The work builds on sliding-window anchoring in RPN-based two-stage detectors and in one-stage detectors (SSD, RetinaNet, YOLOv2), on FPN multi-level feature maps, and on focal loss for imbalanced anchors; the claimed gap is that prior methods, including cascade and anchor-free variants, still rely on dense uniform anchors and none has explored sparse, feature-guided anchoring.

evidence.quote: previous methods (singlestage, two-stage and multi-stage) still rely on dense and uniform anchors by sliding window.
We discard the sliding window scheme and propose a better counterpart to guide the anchoring and generate sparse anchors, which has not been explored before.

solution.summary: Guided Anchoring factorizes the anchor distribution into a location term and a conditional shape term: one branch predicts an object-center probability map from which sparse anchor locations are selected, another predicts a per-location (w, h), and a feature-adaption module deformably convolves features to match the predicted anchor shapes; high-quality proposals from this RPN can then fine-tune trained detectors.
solution.approach: Jointly predict anchor center probabilities and location-dependent anchor shapes from semantic features, then adapt features to those shapes with a deformable-convolution offset field.
components: anchor location prediction branch (1x1 convolution + sigmoid objectness map, thresholded for sparsity)
anchor shape prediction branch with log-space transform w = sigma * s * exp(dw), h = sigma * s * exp(dh)
anchor-guided feature adaptation implemented as a 3x3 deformable convolution driven by predicted shapes
masked convolution on excluded regions for more efficient inference
multi-level anchor generation with parameters shared across FPN levels
center/ignore/outside region targets for location training with focal loss
vIoU-based shape targets approximated by 9 sampled (w, h) pairs and a bounded-IoU-style shape loss
fine-tuning schedule that replaces RPN with pre-computed GA-RPN proposals for 3 epochs

evidence.quote: we present an alternative scheme, named Guided Anchoring, which leverages semantic features to guide the anchoring.
The proposed method jointly predicts the locations where the center of objects of interest are likely to exist as well as the scales and aspect ratios at different locations.
On top of predicted anchor shapes, we mitigate the feature inconsistency with a feature adaption module.
we further introduce a feature adaptation module, which adapts the feature according to the anchor shape.
we adopt a 3 × 3 deformable convolutional layer [4] to implement NT .

experiments.summary: Evaluation is on MS COCO 2017 (train split, val for ablations, test-dev for detection), measuring proposal recall (AR100/AR300/AR1000 and AR by size) for GA-RPN against RPN and prior proposal methods, and detection AP after integrating guided anchoring into Fast R-CNN, Faster R-CNN and RetinaNet, plus ablations of each module, the location threshold and proposal fine-tuning.

benchmarks.split: test-dev, fine-tuned Faster R-CNN with GA-RPN proposals

evidence.quote: With Guided Anchoring, we achieve 9.1% higher recall on MS COCO with 90% fewer anchors than the RPN baseline.
Specifically, it improves AR300 by 10.5% and AR1000 by 9.1% respectively.
it improves a fully converged Faster R-CNN model from 37.4% to 39.6%, in only 3 epochs.
The shape prediction branch is shown effective which leads to a gain of 4.2%.

limitations.summary: The location branch adds only marginal recall, the speed benefit is limited because the RPN head is a single convolution, exploiting high-quality proposals requires re-tuning training thresholds rather than dropping them in as-is, and the analytic vIoU objective is too hard to implement exactly so it is approximated by sampled shapes.
items: The location prediction branch brings only marginal accuracy improvement; its value is sparsity and efficiency.
Speedup from fewer anchors is not apparent with the current single-layer RPN head.
Simply replacing RPN with GA-RPN and keeping the old training settings gives less than 1 point of gain.
The exact vIoU objective is complicated and is only approximated by sampling 9 (w, h) pairs.

evidence.quote: The location prediction branch brings marginal improvement.
It is noteworthy that the head in RPN is just one convolutional layer, so the speedup is not apparent.
adopting exactly the same settings as before can only bring limited gain (e.g.,
the analytic expression of vIoU(awh , gt) is complicated, and hard to be implemented efficiently in an end-to-end network.

futureDirections.direction: Exploit the anchor sparsity for faster inference by pairing it with a heavier detection head than the current single-convolution RPN head.
futureDirections.quote: Nevertheless, a significant reduction in the number of anchors offers a possibility to perform more efficient inference with a heavier head.

equations.name: Anchor distribution factorization
equations.expr: p(x, y, w, h|I) = p(x, y|I) * p(w, h|x, y, I)

equations.name: Anchor shape transform
equations.expr: w = sigma * s * exp(dw); h = sigma * s * exp(dh)

equations.name: Joint multi-task loss
equations.expr: L = lambda1 * Lloc + lambda2 * Lshape + Lcls + Lreg

equations.name: vIoU
equations.expr: vIoU(awh, gt) = max over w>0,h>0 of IoUnormal(awh, gt)
